# Pertinence des actes d’imagerie cervicale chez l’adulte en cas de cervicalgie non traumatique ou après un traumatisme cervical
## **Pertinence de l’imagerie cervicale en cas de cervicalgie après un traumatisme cervical non pénétrant chez l’adulte**
Les traumatismes non pénétrants du rachis cervical représentent un motif fréquent de consultation aux urgences.
Seuls 2 à 3 % des personnes, sans trouble de conscience, consultant pour un traumatisme du rachis cervical présentent des lésions « significatives » du rachis. La cervicalgie, fréquente, évolue favorablement dans environ la moitié des cas.
* En cas de cervicalgie après un traumatisme cervical non pénétrant, dans le contexte de l’urgence, l’imagerie cervicale est indiquée **:**

# Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease: recognition, diagnosis and management
## Recommendations
[Making decisions using NICE guidelines](https://www.nice.org.uk/about/what-we-do/our-programmes/nice-guidance/nice-guidelines/using-NICE-guidelines-to-make-decisions) explains how we use words to show the strength (or certainty) of our recommendations, and has information about prescribing medicines (including off-label use), professional guidelines, standards and laws (including on consent and mental capacity), and safeguarding.

...

### 1.1 Recognising bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease
#### When to suspect bacterial meningitis
##### 1.1.4
[Strongly suspect](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) bacterial meningitis in people with all the symptoms in the red flag combination:
* fever
* headache
* neck stiffness
* altered level of consciousness or cognition (including confusion or delirium).

...

##### 1.1.6
Suspect bacterial meningitis based on assessment of the symptoms and signs in table 1 (for babies, children and young people) or table 2 (for adults), and the [section on risk factors](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) . Take into account that:
* bacterial meningitis can present with any of these symptoms and signs
* the more symptoms and signs a person has, the more likely it is that they have bacterial meningitis.

##### 1.1.7
If you suspect or strongly suspect bacterial meningitis, transfer the person to hospital as an emergency (see the [recommendations on transfer to hospital](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) ).

...

For more guidance on assessing for sepsis, see the [section on evaluating risk in NICE's guidelines on suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng253/chapter/Evaluating-risk) , [suspected sepsis in under 16s](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng254/chapter/Evaluating-risk-level) and [suspected sepsis in pregnant or recently pregnant people](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng255/chapter/Evaluating-risk-level) . |
| **Neurological** | – |

...

| Fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered level of consciousness or cognition (including confusion or delirium) | Fever and neck stiffness are less common in babies. Headache and neck stiffness are harder to identify in babies and [young children](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) . See recommendations 1.1.4 to 1.1.6 on when to strongly suspect or suspect bacterial meningitis. |
| **Appearance** | – |
| Bulging fontanelle | In babies and young children with an open fontanelle. |
| Headache | Fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered level of consciousness or cognition are the red flag combination for bacterial meningitis. Babies and children and [young people](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) with cognitive impairment or communication difficulties may not be able to report headache. |

...

| Symptoms and signs in adults | Notes |
| **Red flag combination** | – |
| Fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered level of consciousness or cognition (including confusion or delirium) | Fever is less common in [older adults](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) . Headache and neck stiffness are harder to identify in adults with cognitive impairment. Neck stiffness is harder to identify in adults with dementia or arthritis. Altered level of consciousness or cognition may be missed in [young adults](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) and older adults. See recommendations 1.1.4 to 1.1.6 on when to strongly suspect or suspect bacterial meningitis. |
| **Appearance** | – |

| **Behaviour** | – |
| Irritability | – |
| Lethargy | Common in older adults. |

...

#### When to suspect meningococcal disease
##### 1.1.13
| Symptom or sign | Notes |
| **Red flags** | – |
| Haemorrhagic, non-blanching rash with lesions larger than 2 mm (purpura) Rapidly progressive and/or spreading non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash Any symptoms and signs of bacterial meningitis (see [tables 1 and 2](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) ), when combined with a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash | Check all over the body and look for petechiae in the conjunctivae. Rashes may be difficult to see on brown, black or tanned skin. |
| **Non-specific symptom or sign** | – |
| **Appearance** | – |
| Lethargy, does not wake or if roused does not stay awake | Common in babies, [young children](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) and older adults. |

...

### 1.2 Transfer to hospital and antibiotics before arrival at hospital
#### 1.2.6
Do not give antibiotics outside of hospital if the person has [severe antibiotic allergy](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) to either ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin.

...

### 1.4 Investigating suspected bacterial meningitis in hospital
#### Timing of investigations and antibiotics
##### 1.4.1
* blood tests and lumbar puncture are performed before starting antibiotics (if it is safe to do so and will not cause a clinically significant delay to starting antibiotics), and in line with the [sections on blood tests](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) and [lumbar puncture](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) .

...

#### Neuroimaging
##### 1.4.6
Do not routinely perform neuroimaging before lumbar puncture.

##### 1.4.7
Perform imaging if the person has:
* risk factors for an evolving space-occupying lesion **or**
* any of these symptoms or signs, which might indicate raised intracranial pressure:
  + abnormal pupillary reactions
  + a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 9 or less, or a progressive and sustained or rapid fall in level of consciousness.
    Do not perform a lumbar puncture until these factors have been resolved.

##### 1.4.8
Take bloods, give antibiotics and stabilise the person before imaging.

...

#### Lumbar puncture
##### 1.4.10
If the person has started on antibiotics before having a lumbar puncture, perform a lumbar puncture as soon as possible (if it is safe to perform).

...

##### 1.4.12
* extensive or rapidly spreading purpura
* infection at the lumbar puncture site
* risk factors for an evolving space-occupying lesion (follow [recommendation 1.4.7 on imaging](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) )
* any of these symptoms or signs, which might indicate raised intracranial pressure (follow recommendation 1.4.7 on imaging):
+ abnormal pupillary reactions

...

### 1.5 Investigating suspected meningococcal disease in hospital
#### Timing of investigations and antibiotics
##### 1.5.1
* antibiotics start within 1 hour of the person with suspected meningococcal disease arriving at hospital, and in line with the [section on antibiotics for meningococcal disease in hospital](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) .
* blood tests are performed before starting antibiotics, and in line with the [section on blood tests](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) .

...

### 1.6 Antibiotics for bacterial meningitis in hospital
#### 1.6.2
If it is safe to do so and will not cause a clinically significant delay to starting antibiotics, perform a lumbar puncture before giving antibiotics (see the [sections on lumbar puncture](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) and [cerebrospinal fluid investigations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) ).

...

#### Before the causative organism is known, or when it cannot be identified
##### 1.6.5
For suspected bacterial meningitis when the causative organism has not been identified:
* give ceftriaxone (use the [highest doses recommended by the BNF](https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drugs/ceftriaxone/) or [BNFC](https://bnfc.nice.org.uk/drugs/ceftriaxone/) or refer to local antimicrobial guidance)
* if ceftriaxone is contraindicated, consider cefotaxime (see the BNFC for contraindications to ceftriaxone for pre-term babies under 41 weeks corrected gestational age).

...

##### 1.6.9
* continue antibiotics for 10 days
* after 10 days, stop antibiotics if the person has recovered, or get advice from an infection specialist if they have not.

...

#### When the causative organism is known
##### Streptococcus pneumoniae
###### 1.6.10
* after 10 days, stop antibiotics if the person has recovered, or get advice from an [infection specialist](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) if they have not.

...

##### Haemophilus influenzae type b
###### 1.6.11
* after 7 days, stop antibiotics if the person has recovered, or continue for a total of 10 days if they have not
* get further advice from an infection specialist if the person has not recovered after 10 days.

...

##### Group B streptococcal meningitis
###### 1.6.12
* after 14 days, stop antibiotics if the person has recovered, or get further advice from an infection specialist if they have not.

...

##### Enterobacterales (coliforms)
###### 1.6.13
* get advice from an infection specialist on using meropenem as an alternative to ceftriaxone and cefotaxime, while awaiting antibiotic sensitivities
* review treatment once antibiotic sensitivities are available
* after 21 days, stop antibiotics if the person has recovered, or get further advice from an infection specialist if they have not.

...

##### Listeria monocytogenes
###### 1.6.14
* give intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin for 21 days
* get advice from an infection specialist on adding intravenous co-trimoxazole for the first 7 days
* after 21 days, stop antibiotics if the person has recovered, or get advice from an infection specialist if they have not.
In March 2024, this was an off-label use of co-trimoxazole.

...

##### Neisseria meningitidis
###### 1.6.15
* after 5 days, stop antibiotics if the person has recovered, or get advice from an infection specialist if they have not.

...

### 1.7 Antibiotics for meningococcal disease in hospital
#### 1.7.2
After 5 days, stop antibiotics if the person has recovered, or get advice from an [infection specialist](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) if they have not.

...

### 1.12 Preparing for hospital discharge
#### Providing information
##### 1.12.13
* when they are likely to be able to resume:
+ driving (see the [Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency guidance on assessing fitness to drive](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/assessing-fitness-to-drive-a-guide-for-medical-professionals) , including the [advice specific to neurological disorders](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/neurological-disorders-assessing-fitness-to-drive) )
+ travel
+ work and education
+ exercise and sports

...

### 1.13 Care after hospital discharge
#### Further reviews for babies, children and young people
##### 1.13.9
* their child or young person has had meningitis or meningococcal disease
* this may affect their learning
* they may need additional reviews of their educational outcomes and learning needs, even when there have been no known complications.

...

### Terms used in this guideline
#### Strongly suspected
* if the person has the red flag combination of symptoms (see [recommendation 1.1.4](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) ) **or**
* based on clinical assessment of the symptoms and signs and risk factors present, for people who do not have the red flag combination.

...

* if the person has any of the red flag symptoms (see [recommendation 1.1.9](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/recommendations) ) **or**
* based on clinical assessment of the symptoms and signs and risk factors present, for people who do not have any of the red flag symptoms.
